claims.text: Phase homogeneity is the primary determinant of whether CrFeCoNiX alloys form and maintain a protective oxide layer above 900 °C.
A single-phase solid solution provides uniform diffusion pathways.
A single-phase solid solution promotes uniform surface segregation of Si or Al.
Si can form a stable protective SiO2 scale in these alloys.
Al can oxidize to form Al2O3 in a Cr-Fe-Co-Ni-containing high-entropy alloy.
SiO2 or Al2O3 scales formed on these alloys accommodate thermal strain and remain coherent.
Multiphase alloys have heterogeneous local compositions that disrupt uniform oxide formation.
Phase boundaries and compositional inhomogeneity produce localized oxide-scale stresses.
Localized oxide-scale stresses cause cracking and spallation.
Microstructural homogeneity governs whether elemental segregation and diffusion produce a continuous oxide scale.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiAl alloys will develop continuous, adherent, and stable oxide layers during exposure above 900 °C.
Multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys will exhibit more oxide cracking and spallation than corresponding single-phase alloys.
Mn is less likely than Si or Al to form a protective oxide scale in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys are expected to form less coherent and more defect-prone oxide layers under identical exposure conditions.
The proposed phase-homogeneity mechanism applies in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Oxide thickness, strain accommodation, and spallation rate may depend on composition, processing, environment, minor alloying elements, and thermal gradients.
